hints: Look at the right-hand side of the graph where substrate concentration is very high. Which inhibitor curve eventually catches up to the no-inhibitor curve, and which one stays much lower?
Remember that adding lots more substrate can outcompete an inhibitor for the active site, but it cannot fix an enzyme that has been changed in shape at a different binding site.
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph is telling you**

Look carefully at the maximum rate (the flat top of each curve). Inhibitor X eventually reaches the same maximum rate as the enzyme with no inhibitor when substrate is high. Inhibitor Y levels off at a much lower maximum rate and never catches up.

This difference in Vmax is your biggest clue.

**Link the pattern to competitive vs non-competitive**

A competitive inhibitor fits into the active site because it has a similar shape to the substrate. If you add lots of substrate, the substrate wins and the normal Vmax is still reached, it just takes more substrate.

A non-competitive inhibitor binds to a site other than the active site (the allosteric site). It changes the shape of the active site, so even with lots of substrate the enzyme cannot work normally and Vmax is permanently lowered.

**Identify X and Y**

Because X reaches the normal Vmax, X must be the competitive inhibitor. Because Y has a lowered Vmax that cannot be overcome, Y must be the non-competitive inhibitor that binds elsewhere.

So Y is non-competitive and binds to a site other than the active site.

options.A: X does reach normal Vmax so it is competitive, but competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, not to another site.
options.B: X is not non-competitive because its Vmax is not lowered, and non-competitive inhibitors do not fit the active site.
options.C: Y has a permanently lowered Vmax so it cannot be competitive, even though the description of shape is correct for a competitive inhibitor.
options.D: Y never reaches normal Vmax, so it is non-competitive, and non-competitive inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site and change enzyme shape.
